title: Bohr's Model, Energy Levels and Shells
summary: How Bohr improved the atomic model, his postulates, the energy levels (shells) and how many electrons each can hold.

p: Dalton (1803) pictured atoms as solid, indivisible spheres, but could not explain their inside. Thomson (1897) found the electron and proposed the 'plum pudding' model. Rutherford (1911) showed from his gold-foil experiment that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it, but his model could not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus or why atoms give out light of only certain colours. Bohr (1913) improved on this by saying that electrons can have only certain fixed amounts of energy.
1. Electrons move around the nucleus in fixed paths (orbits or shells) and do not lose energy while in them. These are called stationary states.
2. Each shell has a fixed energy. The shells nearest the nucleus have the lowest energy; shells farther out have more.

3. An electron can jump between shells. If it absorbs energy it jumps to a higher shell (an excited state). When it falls back it gives out the energy as light (a photon). This explains why each element gives its own line spectrum.
4. The energy absorbed or given out is ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν, where h is Planck's constant (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) and ν is the frequency of the light.
The shells are named K (n = 1), L (n = 2), M (n = 3), N (n = 4), and then O, P, Q. A shell with number n can hold at most 2n² electrons: K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18, N holds 32.
In the first twenty elements, electrons fill the shells in order, but the M shell is treated as full when it holds 8, so the next electrons go into the N shell (for example, calcium is 2, 8, 8, 2).

title: Electronic Configuration and Subshells
summary: Subshells s, p, d and f, the rules for filling them (Aufbau, Pauli, Hund), examples, and why configuration explains valency and the periodic table.

p: Each shell is divided into subshells called s, p, d and f. An s subshell holds up to 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14. The K shell has only 1s. The L shell has 2s and 2p. The M shell has 3s, 3p and 3d.

Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first. Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they spin in opposite directions. Hund's rule: electrons go into orbitals of equal energy one at a time before they pair up.
Order of filling: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p. Notice that 4s fills before 3d.
Study the table. Write the full configuration as subshells and as shell numbers.

Valency: sodium (2, 8, 1) has one outer electron, so its valency is 1; oxygen (2, 6) needs two more, so its valency is 2. Chemical properties: elements with the same outer configuration are in the same group. The period number equals the number of occupied shells, and the group number is linked to the number of outer electrons. Stability of noble gases: neon (2, 8) and argon (2, 8, 8) have full outer shells and are very unreactive. Group 1 metals have one loosely held outer electron, so they react readily; noble gases have full shells, so they hardly react.

title: Ionic Bonding
summary: Why atoms bond, the octet rule, how ionic bonds form by transfer of electrons, examples, and the properties of ionic compounds.

p: Except for the noble gases, atoms are not stable on their own because their outer shells are not full. To become stable they join with other atoms. This is chemical bonding. The octet rule says that atoms gain, lose or share electrons until they have eight electrons in the outer shell, like a noble gas. Hydrogen and helium need only two (the duplet rule).

An ionic bond forms when one atom, usually a metal, gives one or more electrons to another atom, usually a non-metal. The atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion (cation). The atom that gains them becomes a negative ion (anion). The strong force of attraction between the opposite charges is the ionic bond.

Conditions: a large difference in electronegativity (roughly more than 1.7); usually a metal from Group 1, 2 or 3 and a non-metal from Group 15, 16 or 17 (old numbering: groups 5, 6, 7); the metal has a low ionisation energy and the non-metal a high electron affinity.

Sodium chloride, NaCl: sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ (2, 8). Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The ions attract each other and pack in a giant lattice.
Magnesium oxide, MgO: Mg (2, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺; O (2, 6) gains 2 to form O²⁻.
Calcium fluoride, CaF₂: Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺; each F (2, 7) gains 1 electron to form F⁻, so two F⁻ are needed.

img.alt: Three panels: sodium giving an electron to chlorine to make Na+ and Cl-; two hydrogen atoms sharing a pair of electrons; and a water molecule with oxygen sharing electrons with two hydrogens
img.cap: Ionic bonding (left) and covalent bonding (middle and right).

p: They are crystalline solids at room temperature. They have high melting and boiling points because the lattice is strong. Most dissolve in water (a polar solvent) but not in petrol or benzene. They do not conduct electricity as solids (the ions cannot move) but do when molten or dissolved (the ions are free). They are hard but brittle: if the layers of the lattice slip, like charges meet and repel and the crystal cracks.

title: Covalent Bonding and Comparison with Ionic Bonding
summary: How atoms share electrons, single, double, triple and coordinate bonds, examples and properties, and a table comparing ionic and covalent compounds.

p: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that each gets a full outer shell. It happens mainly between non-metals, when the difference in electronegativity is small (less than about 1.7).
Single bond: one shared pair. Hydrogen, H–H. Each hydrogen gives one electron.
Double bond: two shared pairs. Oxygen, O=O. Each oxygen shares two electrons.
Triple bond: three shared pairs. Nitrogen, N≡N.

Coordinate (dative) bond: both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom. Example: the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ is made when the nitrogen of ammonia (NH₃) gives its lone pair to a hydrogen ion (H⁺). Once formed, a coordinate bond is just like any other covalent bond.

Water, H₂O: oxygen (2, 6) shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms. Methane, CH₄: carbon (2, 4) shares one pair with each of four hydrogens. Carbon dioxide, CO₂: carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, so there are two double bonds (O=C=O).

They are usually gases (O₂, CO₂), liquids (water) or soft solids (sulphur, iodine). Melting and boiling points are low because the forces between molecules are weak (the bonds inside each molecule are strong). Exceptions are giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon dioxide, which have very high melting points. Many do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents, though some small polar molecules such as sugar and ethanol do dissolve in water. They do not conduct electricity because there are no free ions or electrons (graphite is an exception because it has free (delocalised) electrons). Covalent bonds are directional, joining particular atoms.

p: Both are made only of carbon. In diamond, each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network, so it is very hard and does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon is bonded to three others in flat layers, with one electron per atom free to move. The layers slide easily (so graphite is soft and used in pencils) and the free electrons let it conduct electricity.

It explains why matter is stable and why salt dissolves in water but oil does not, why water is a liquid and why metals conduct. It guides the design of ceramics, plastics and semiconductors, and is the basis of proteins, carbohydrates and DNA.

title: Oxidation and Reduction
summary: Three ways to define oxidation and reduction (oxygen and hydrogen, electrons, oxidation number) with simple examples, and why they always occur together.

p: In many reactions electrons move from one substance to another. These are oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. They are important in breathing and photosynthesis, extracting metals, batteries, rusting and water treatment.
Oxidation is the addition of oxygen or the removal of hydrogen. Reduction is the removal of oxygen or the addition of hydrogen.
Example 1: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Magnesium is oxidised (it gains oxygen). (The source notes wrote the product as MgO₂, which is wrong; magnesium oxide is MgO.)
Example 2: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Copper(II) oxide is reduced (loses oxygen); hydrogen is oxidised (gains oxygen).
Oxidation is loss of electrons. Reduction is gain of electrons. Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Examples: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (sodium is oxidised). Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (chlorine is reduced).

Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number. Examples: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻: iron goes from +2 to +3, so it is oxidised. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻: chlorine goes from 0 to −1, so it is reduced.

Simple rules for oxidation numbers: an uncombined element is 0; a simple ion has its charge (Na⁺ is +1); oxygen is usually −2; hydrogen is usually +1; the numbers in a compound add up to 0, and in an ion to the charge.

In a redox reaction, oxidation and reduction happen at the same time. The substance that is oxidised is the reducing agent (it gives electrons). The substance that is reduced is the oxidising agent (it takes electrons).

Example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc loses electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation; zinc is the reducing agent). Copper ions gain them: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent). In the picture, a blue copper sulphate solution slowly becomes colourless as a brown layer of copper forms on the zinc.

title: Redox Agents, Examples and Balancing
summary: Common oxidising and reducing agents, types of redox reaction, two ways to balance a redox equation, uses and common mistakes.

p: An oxidising agent (oxidant) accepts electrons and is itself reduced. Examples: oxygen, chlorine, potassium manganate(VII), potassium dichromate(VI) and nitric acid. A reducing agent (reductant) gives electrons and is itself oxidised. Examples: hydrogen, carbon monoxide, sodium, zinc and iron.

Combination: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O. Displacement: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (carbon goes from −4 to +4, oxidised; oxygen goes from 0 to −2, reduced). Corrosion (rusting): 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, which changes to hydrated iron(III) oxide, rust.

sections.h: Balancing by the oxidation number method
p: 1. Give oxidation numbers to every element. 2. Find which change up (oxidation) and which change down (reduction). 3. Make the total electrons lost equal the total electrons gained. 4. Balance the rest of the atoms and charges.

Example: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Each Na goes from 0 to +1 (loses 1 electron, 2 Na lose 2 electrons). Cl₂ goes from 0 to −1 for each of 2 atoms (gains 2 electrons). The electrons balance, so the equation is balanced.

1. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations separately. 2. Balance atoms other than H and O. 3. Balance O by adding H₂O. 4. Balance H by adding H⁺ (in acid). 5. Balance charge by adding electrons. 6. Multiply so the electrons are equal, add the two half-equations and cancel the electrons.

Example in acid: Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ → Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺. Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 and add: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
More practice answers: 3H₂S + 2HNO₃ → 3S + 2NO + 4H₂O. MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. 3Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + 8H⁺ → 3Cu²⁺ + 2NO + 4H₂O. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3SO₂ + 2H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻ + H₂O.

Living things: respiration oxidises glucose to carbon dioxide and water and releases energy; photosynthesis reduces carbon dioxide to glucose. Industry: iron is made by reducing iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide; electroplating and electrolysis; making bleaches. Environment: chlorine kills germs in water. Everyday life: rusting is an unwanted redox reaction; batteries (dry cells, lead-acid, lithium-ion) use redox reactions to make electricity.

Thinking oxidation always means adding oxygen. It may be loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number. Forgetting that oxidation and reduction always occur together. Mixing up the agents: the oxidising agent is the substance that is reduced, and the reducing agent is the substance that is oxidised.

title: Water: Importance and Properties
summary: Why water matters to living things, industry and the home, its physical properties and its chemical reactions with metals, non-metals and electricity.

p: Water is the most plentiful compound on Earth and is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many things. It occurs as ice, liquid water and water vapour.

Biological: carries nutrients and waste in plants and animals; sweating and evaporation cool the body; it is needed for photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Industrial: raw material for hydrogen, oxygen and acids; a coolant in power plants and engines; used for cleaning and dissolving. Domestic: drinking, cooking, washing and sanitation.

Pure water is colourless, odourless and tasteless. It boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C at 1 atmosphere. Its density is greatest, 1 g/cm³, at 4 °C. Water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense and floats; fish survive under ice in cold lakes. It has a high specific heat capacity: it takes in or gives out much heat for a small change in temperature, which makes the climate near the sea milder. It has a high surface tension because of hydrogen bonding, so small insects can walk on it. Pure water hardly conducts electricity, but natural water does because of dissolved ions.

With metals: active metals (sodium, potassium, calcium) react with cold water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Less reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc react with steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.
With non-metals: chlorine dissolves in water to give hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid (HOCl): Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl.
Hydrolysis: some salts react with water; ammonium chloride solution is slightly acidic.
Electrolysis: when electricity is passed through acidified water, it decomposes: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen is collected, by volume.

Water with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts does not lather easily with soap and is called hard water. Boiling can remove temporary hardness (due to hydrogencarbonates). Rainwater and distilled water are soft.

title: Solutions and Solubility
summary: Solute, solvent and solution, the types of solutions, their properties, what solubility is and the factors that affect it.

p: A solution is a uniform (homogeneous) mixture of two or more substances. The substance that dissolves is the solute (usually the smaller amount). The substance that does the dissolving is the solvent (usually the larger amount). Examples: salt (solute) in water (solvent); sugar in water.
By state: solid solutions (brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin), liquid solutions (vinegar, sugar solution) and gaseous solutions (air).

By how much solute is dissolved: an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature. A saturated solution holds the most solute it can at that temperature; extra solute stays undissolved. A supersaturated solution holds more solute than normal. It is made by dissolving a lot of solute in a hot solution and cooling it carefully without disturbing it, and is unstable: a small crystal or a tap causes crystals to appear.
By electrical conduction: electrolytic solutions conduct (salt solution, hydrochloric acid) and non-electrolytic solutions do not (sugar in water, ethanol in water).

img.alt: Three beakers showing an unsaturated solution with all solute dissolved, a saturated solution with undissolved solid at the bottom, and a supersaturated solution with crystals forming around a seed crystal

p: They are uniform throughout. The particles are the size of molecules or ions, so cannot be seen. They are clear (transparent) and do not scatter a beam of light. The solute cannot be removed by filtration, but can be recovered by evaporation or distillation. They may be dilute (little solute) or concentrated (much solute).

Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature to make a saturated solution. It is measured in g per 100 g of solvent (at a stated temperature). Example: the solubility of sodium chloride is about 36 g per 100 g of water at 25 °C. (In more advanced work, solubility is also given in mol/dm³, the SI-based unit.)

1. Nature of solute and solvent: 'like dissolves like'. Polar and ionic solutes (salt, sugar) dissolve in polar solvents (water). Non-polar solutes (iodine, fats, oil) dissolve in non-polar solvents (tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, or kerosene). This is why sugar dissolves in water but not in kerosene.
2. Temperature: for most solids, solubility rises as the temperature rises (potassium nitrate). For gases, solubility falls when temperature rises: a warm soft drink loses its fizz.
3. Pressure: has little effect on solids and liquids, but the solubility of a gas rises with pressure (Henry's law). Soft drinks are bottled under CO₂ pressure and fizz when opened.

4. Particle size: small particles dissolve faster because of the larger surface area. 5. Stirring makes a solute dissolve faster, but does not change how much can dissolve in total. 6. Impurities may change solubility.

title: Solubility Curves and Crystallisation
summary: How to read a solubility curve, solubility calculations, how to measure solubility, and how to grow crystals of pure substances.

p: Aim: find the solubility of potassium nitrate (KNO₃) in water at 40 °C. Apparatus: beaker, thermometer, balance, stirrer, heat source, evaporating dish.
Method: weigh 100 g of water into a beaker and warm it to 40 °C. Add KNO₃ little by little, stirring, until no more dissolves (the solution is saturated). Record the mass of solute added.

Solubility = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solvent) × 100. If 50 g dissolve in 100 g of water at 40 °C, solubility = (50 ÷ 100) × 100 = 50 g per 100 g of water. (Our standard value for KNO₃ at 40 °C is 64 g per 100 g of water; the 50 g was only an example.)

A solubility curve is a graph of solubility (g per 100 g of water, vertical axis) against temperature (°C, horizontal axis). For most salts, such as KNO₃, the curve slopes upward, because the solubility rises with temperature. For gases, it slopes downward. A point on the curve is a saturated solution. A point below the curve is unsaturated. A point above the curve means more solute than can dissolve (it would appear as undissolved solid, or as a supersaturated solution if cooled carefully).
Uses: read the solubility at any temperature; find the temperature at which a solution becomes saturated; calculate how much solute crystallises when a solution cools; compare solutes.

img.alt: A rising solubility curve of potassium nitrate from 13 g per 100 g of water at 0 degrees to 150 g at 80 degrees, with marked points at 20 degrees (32 g) and 40 degrees (64 g) and the regions unsaturated below and supersaturated above
img.cap: Solubility curve of potassium nitrate (values rounded for teaching).

p: Example 1: a saturated solution at 40 °C holds 64 g of KNO₃ per 100 g of water. At 20 °C the solubility is 32 g. If the solution is cooled to 20 °C, the mass that crystallises = 64 − 32 = 32 g (for each 100 g of water).
Example 2: at 80 °C, 150 g of KNO₃ dissolves in 100 g of water. At 30 °C the solubility is 45 g. Mass that crystallises = 150 − 45 = 105 g.
Example 3: the solubility of NaCl at 25 °C is 36 g per 100 g of water. How much NaCl is needed for a saturated solution in 250 g of water? Mass = 36 ÷ 100 × 250 = 90 g.
Example 4: 90 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 100 g of water at 60 °C, where the solubility is 110 g per 100 g. Since 90 < 110, the solution is unsaturated (it can take 20 g more).

Example 5: the solubility of KCl is 45 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 30 g at 20 °C. How much KCl crystallises when 100 g of saturated solution at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C? A saturated solution at 60 °C has 45 g KCl in 145 g of solution, so 100 g of solution holds 100 × 45 ÷ 145 = 31.0 g KCl and 69.0 g of water. At 20 °C, 69.0 g of water can hold 69.0 × 30 ÷ 100 = 20.7 g. So the mass crystallising = 31.0 − 20.7 = 10.3 g.
Crystallisation is the formation of pure solid crystals from a solution by cooling it or by evaporating some of the solvent. It is used to purify solids.

Making crystals of copper(II) sulphate in the laboratory: 1. Dissolve excess copper(II) sulphate in hot water to make a saturated solution. 2. Filter it to remove undissolved solid and impurities. 3. Let it cool slowly; crystals form because the solubility falls. 4. Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold water, and dry them between sheets of filter paper. Slow cooling gives large, well-shaped crystals.
Industrial uses: refining sugar, purifying salt, making alum, drugs and fertilisers.

Drug design (how much of a drug dissolves in the blood), food and drink making, oxygen dissolved in water that fish need to breathe (warm water holds less oxygen), the manufacture of fertilisers, soaps and carbonated drinks, and purification of chemicals.
